pos: n. (Hincmar, c. 806–882, archbishop of Reims from 845, prosecutor of Gottschalk and author of the Quierzy articles of 853)
etymology: Old Frankish personal name, from hin, of uncertain sense, and mar, famous.
biblical_def: Hincmar was archbishop of Reims for thirty-seven years and the most powerful churchman of the West Frankish kingdom under Charles the Bald. He is remembered chiefly as the man who silenced Gottschalk of Orbais. At the synod of Quierzy in 849 he had Gottschalk condemned, flogged until he cast his own writings into the fire, and shut up for the rest of his life in the monastery of Hautvillers. In 853 a second synod at Quierzy adopted four articles of Hincmar's drafting: that God predestined the elect to life but did not predestine any to punishment, that the free will lost in Adam is restored by grace, that God wills all men to be saved, and that Christ suffered for all. The church of Lyon answered him, and the synod of Valence in 855 rejected his articles. Hincmar also resisted the forged Pseudo-Isidorean decretals when Pope Nicholas I used them against his authority. The text he leaned on was the universal will of 1Ti 2:4, that God “will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4). The text he could not answer was Christ's own word to unbelievers: “ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep” (John 10:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and predestination as the decree of God by which he has foreordained all things.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. In church history, a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
PREDESTINA'TION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events; the decree of God by which he hath, from eternity, unchangeably appointed or determined whatever comes to pass.
ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class, a metropolitan bishop.
scriptures: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.
John 10:26
But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you.
Rom 9:22
What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: The bishop who answered Augustinian predestination with flogging and four articles of universal grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Hincmar's articles are the Carolingian form of the semi-Pelagian settlement, and the dictionary names them so. Predestination to life without any predestination to death leaves the non-elect in a state God did not decree; a universal saving will that does not save leaves God willing what does not come to pass; a death of Christ for all that redeems none in particular empties the purchase of Act 20:28, where the church is the flock God “hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). Rom 9:22 speaks of “the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Rom 9:22) without embarrassment.

The method was worse than the doctrine. A monk who asked to prove his teaching by ordeal was answered with the lash, and the archbishop who would not debate him commissioned John Scotus Eriugena to refute him, and so produced a treatise worse than anything Gottschalk wrote. What is honourable in Hincmar is his resistance to the forged decretals and to papal interference in the Frankish churches. What is mourned is that the West's ablest bishop used his authority to make Augustine's doctrine of grace a crime.
roots_summary: Greek thelo (G2309), to will; skeuos (G4632), vessel; peripoieo (G4046), to purchase.
roots_lines: Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to desire; 1 Timothy 2:4.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to fit, to make ready; Romans 9:22.
usage: “will have all men to be saved” (1Ti 2:4) — the text Quierzy built upon.
“ye are not of my sheep” (John 10:26) — the text it never answered.
“purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — a definite flock and a definite price.

pos: n. (Amolo, archbishop of Lyon 841–852, successor of Agobard, who wrote to Gottschalk during the predestination quarrel)
etymology: Frankish personal name, a diminutive of the root amal, labour, vigour.
biblical_def: Amolo followed Agobard as archbishop of Lyon in 841 and held the see through the first years of the Carolingian predestination quarrel. When Gottschalk of Orbais was condemned in 849, Hincmar of Reims sent his own account of the case to Lyon, and Amolo answered with a letter addressed to Gottschalk himself. The letter is a careful document. Amolo affirmed what Augustine taught, that God chose His elect by free grace before the world and that none of them perishes, and he rebuked several of Gottschalk's sharper propositions — among them that the baptized who afterward fall away were never truly washed, and that God takes no pleasure in any outward good of the reprobate. He urged the imprisoned monk to submit and to stop writing. What Amolo did not do was endorse Hincmar's universal articles; the church of Lyon under his successors became the chief defender of the doctrine Hincmar was trying to bury. Amolo's instinct was Paul's, that “The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19), and that the same seal reads, “Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity” (2Ti 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines election in theology as the choice of persons to eternal life, and reprobation as the state of being abandoned to destruction.
webster_full: ELEC'TION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven.
REPROBA'TION, n. The act of abandoning, or state of being abandoned to eternal destruction.
EPIS'TLE, n. A writing directed or sent, communicating intelligence to a distant person; a letter.
scriptures: Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
John 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
corruption_summary: A pastoral middle voice in the Gottschalk affair — sound on election, too ready to counsel silence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation Amolo represents is older and quieter: to agree with a persecuted man's doctrine in substance while advising him to stop confessing it. Eph 1:4 says God “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4), and Amolo did not deny it. But a truth that may be held and not spoken has already been handed to the men who wish it unspoken.

The principle to recover is that doctrinal precision and pastoral counsel are not rivals. Amolo was right to correct Gottschalk where he overreached, and right that the golden chain of Rom 8:30 runs from predestination to glory without a broken link: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30). He would have served the church better by saying as plainly to Reims what he said to the prisoner.
roots_summary: Greek ginosko (G1097), to know; eklegomai (G1586), to choose; helko (G1670), to draw.
usage: “The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19) — the seal on the foundation.
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44) — the necessity of grace.
“them he also glorified” (Rom 8:30) — the end of the chain.

pos: n. (Florus, deacon of the church of Lyon, d. c. 860, compiler of Augustine on Paul and opponent of Amalarius and Eriugena)
biblical_def: Florus was a deacon and master of the cathedral school at Lyon, a poet, a canonist, and one of the most learned men of the ninth century. He did three things the church still has reason to remember. He compiled an Exposition of the Epistles of Paul drawn entirely from the works of Augustine, arranging the bishop of Hippo's comments verse by verse, so that the Carolingian church read Romans through Augustine's eyes. He attacked the allegorical liturgy of Amalarius of Metz, whose fanciful explanations of every gesture of the mass he thought a corruption of plain worship, and had it censured at Quierzy in 838. And in 852, writing for the church of Lyon, he answered John Scotus Eriugena's treatise on predestination, which he judged a philosopher's arrogance passing for theology. Florus held that God's predestination is twofold and just, that grace is not earned, and that the Scriptures and the fathers are the judges of dialectic, not its servants. He stood where Paul stood: “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deacon as a church officer subordinate to the presbyter, and dialectics as the art of reasoning or disputing.
webster_full: DEA'CON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders, whose office is to serve in the distribution of the elements and in the care of the poor.
DIALEC'TICS, n. That branch of logic which teaches the rules and modes of reasoning.
EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
corruption_summary: A deacon who made Augustine the reader of Paul and Scripture the judge of philosophy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error Florus fought is the permanent one of letting a borrowed philosophy set the terms on which Scripture may speak. Eriugena reasoned that because God is simple and sin is nothing, God cannot predestine to punishment; Florus answered that this was dialectic sitting in judgment on the apostle. Col 2:8 names the danger: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).

The principle to recover is that grace has a remnant and a reason, and the reason is grace itself: “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). Florus also saw that worship explained by allegory soon becomes worship governed by allegory, and that plainness in the liturgy and plainness in the doctrine of grace are one fidelity.
roots_lines: Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to spoil, carry off as booty; Colossians 2:8.
usage: “but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16) — the ground of the Lyon theology.
“where is the disputer of this world?” (1Co 1:20) — his question to Eriugena.
“a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — election as mercy, not merit.

pos: n. (Remigius, archbishop of Lyon 852–875, who presided over the synod of Valence in 855)
biblical_def: Remigius succeeded Amolo at Lyon in 852 and made his church the chief opponent of Hincmar's articles of Quierzy. A treatise issued in the name of the church of Lyon, usually attributed to him, answered three letters circulated by Hincmar's party and argued that Gottschalk had been condemned unjustly and punished cruelly. In January 855 Remigius presided with Agilmar of Vienne and Ebbo of Grenoble over the synod of Valence. Its canons confessed the predestination of the elect to life, and the predestination of the wicked to death, while insisting that in the condemnation of the wicked their own desert precedes God's just judgment, and that God does not predestine any man to sin. Valence rejected the four articles of Quierzy and dismissed the nineteen propositions of John Scotus Eriugena with contempt as Scots porridge. Remigius sat again at the councils of Langres and Savonnieres in 859 and at Tusey in 860, where an ambiguous compromise ended the quarrel without deciding it. He held Paul's line: “Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council.
webster_full: CAN'ON, n. A law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline in the church.
DESERT', n. That which gives a right to reward or demands punishment; merit or demerit.
scriptures: Rom 9:18
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
John 17:9
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.

But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
corruption_summary: The synod of Valence: double predestination confessed, with the sinner's own guilt kept in view.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The canons of Valence are a model of the care the doctrine requires, and the misuse of the doctrine they guard against is the one its enemies still allege: that to confess reprobation is to make God the author of sin. Valence said the opposite in so many words. Election is not of works, “that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11); reprobation finds the sinner already guilty.

The principle to recover is that Christ's own intercession is particular. “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (John 17:9). Lyon saw that a redemption Christ does not plead for is not the redemption the Scriptures describe, and that the church owes the persecuted Gottschalk an apology Hincmar never offered.
roots_summary: Greek skleruno (G4645), to harden; prothesis (G4286), purpose; haireomai (G138), to choose.
roots_lines: Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting forth, purpose; Romans 9:11.
Greek haireomai (G138) — to take for oneself, choose; 2 Thessalonians 2:13.
usage: “whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18) — the sovereignty Valence confessed.
“I pray not for the world” (John 17:9) — a particular intercession.
“chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit” (2Th 2:13) — the means joined to the end.

pos: n. (Lupus of Ferrieres, c. 805–862, abbot, letter-writer, collector of classical texts, and defender of Gottschalk's doctrine)
etymology: Latin Servatus, preserved, a name he took for his deliverance from danger; Lupus, wolf.
biblical_def: Servatus Lupus, abbot of Ferrieres from 840, was the finest Latin stylist of his generation and the most diligent hunter of books. He had studied under Rabanus Maurus at Fulda, and his surviving letters, more than a hundred and thirty of them, are full of requests to borrow manuscripts of Cicero, Livy, Suetonius, Macrobius, and the fathers so that his monks could copy and correct them. When the predestination quarrel broke out he wrote On Three Questions, addressed to Charles the Bald, setting out the Augustinian answer on each disputed point: that free will after the fall is able to do good only when it is freed by grace, that predestination is twofold, and that the blood of Christ was shed for those who believe and not for the unbelieving world. Lupus wrote without heat and without fear of Hincmar, and he gathered the patristic testimony to show that what Gottschalk taught was not a novelty but Augustine and Prosper. His text for the third question was the angel's announcement of the name of Jesus: “he shall save his people from their sins” (Mat 1:21). He is also a reminder that the Christian love of books is old: Paul asked for “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines redemption as the deliverance of sinners from the bondage of sin and the penalties of God's violated law by the atonement of Christ.
webster_full: REDEMP'TION, n. In theology, the purchase of God's favor by the death and sufferings of Christ; the ransom or deliverance of sinners from the bondage of sin and the penalties of God's violated law.
AB'BOT, n. The head or superior of an abbey or monastery.
MAN'USCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen.
scriptures: Mat 1:21
And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
John 10:15
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: A humanist abbot who defended particular redemption from the fathers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lupus is sometimes treated as a forerunner of the Renaissance and nothing more, as though his love of Cicero and his defense of predestination belonged to two different men. The corruption to refuse is that division. The man who corrected Livy's text did it for the same reason he corrected Hincmar's theology: words matter, and the true reading must be recovered.

The principle to recover is the particularity of the cross. Christ said, “I lay down my life for the sheep” (John 10:15), and Lupus would not let that verse be dissolved into a death for everyone that secures no one. He also knew the Preacher's warning about his own vocation: “of making many books there is no end” (Ecc 12:12).
usage: “he shall save his people from their sins” (Mat 1:21) — the name that defines the work.
“I lay down my life for the sheep” (John 10:15) — his third question answered.
“but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13) — the apostle's own book-hunt.

pos: n. (Johannes Scottus Eriugena, c. 815–c. 877, Irish master at the court of Charles the Bald, author of the Periphyseon)
etymology: Latin Scotus, an Irishman (the medieval sense); Eriugena, coined from Eriu, Ireland, and -gena, born.
biblical_def: John Scotus Eriugena was the most original philosopher of the early Middle Ages and its most dangerous theologian. An Irishman with rare command of Greek, he taught at the palace school of Charles the Bald and translated the writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, which carried Neoplatonism into the Latin West. In 851 Hincmar of Reims asked him to refute Gottschalk. Eriugena's On Divine Predestination argued that predestination is one because God is one, that sin and death are nothing and so cannot be objects of God's decree, and that punishment is the sinner's own self-inflicted torment rather than a place. The book alarmed both sides. Prudentius of Troyes and Florus of Lyons answered it, and the synod of Valence in 855 rejected its propositions as Scots porridge. His later Periphyseon divided all nature into four, from God who creates and is not created to God who neither creates nor is created, and described all things as proceeding from God and returning into Him. Pope Honorius III ordered it burned in 1225. Against it stands Scripture's distinction of Creator and creature, and the indictment of those who “worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator” (Rom 1:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pantheism as the doctrine that the universe is God, and philosophy as the knowledge of the reasons of things.
webster_full: PAN'THEISM, n. The doctrine that the universe is God, or the system of theology in which it is maintained that the universe is the supreme God.
PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom. But in modern acceptation, philosophy is a general term denoting an explanation of the reasons of things.
TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; interpretation.
scriptures: Rom 1:25
Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
corruption_summary: Neoplatonism in Christian dress: predestination dissolved into divine simplicity, creation into emanation.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Eriugena's system as a pantheizing Neoplatonism and a corruption of the doctrine of creation. A God from whom all things proceed and into whom all things return is not the God of Gen 1:1 who made the heavens and the earth out of nothing and remains distinct from them for ever. Rom 1:25 places the blurring of that line at the root of idolatry, among those “Who changed the truth of God into a lie” (Rom 1:25).

His theology of predestination fails for the same reason. By making God's simplicity the premise and the apostle's words the conclusion to be adjusted, he did what Paul warned Timothy against, embracing “oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20). Modern admirers who treat him as a bold free thinker ahead of his age repeat the error; what was ahead of its age was the conviction that reason may correct revelation. The Lyon churchmen who called it porridge were right.
usage: “more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom 1:25) — the line he blurred.
“oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20) — reason set over revelation.
“God is not a man, that he should lie” (Num 23:19) — the God who speaks and is not reasoned away.

pos: n. (Smaragdus, abbot of Saint-Mihiel in Lorraine, d. c. 830, author of the Via Regia and a commentary on the Rule of Benedict)
biblical_def: Smaragdus was abbot of Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse in the reigns of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, a grammarian, homilist, and counsellor of kings. His Via Regia, the King's Way, is one of the first Carolingian mirrors for princes: a short book of counsel urging a Christian ruler to fear God, love justice, defend the poor and the widow, and rule himself before he rules others. His Crown of Monks gathered patristic sayings for the monastic life, his commentary on the Rule of Benedict became a standard guide, and his Collections on the Sunday epistles and gospels supplied preachers with the fathers' comments for the whole church year. In 809, after the council of Aachen debated the addition of filioque to the creed, Smaragdus drew up the dossier of patristic texts that Charlemagne's envoys carried to Pope Leo III. His counsel to kings echoes Moses' law for Israel's king, that the book of the law “shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19), and the psalmist's summons, “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings” (Psa 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a monk as one who retires from the world to devote himself to religion, and a homily as a discourse or sermon read to a congregation.
webster_full: MONK, n. A man who retires from the ordinary temporal concerns of the world, and devotes himself wholly to religion.
HOM'ILY, n. A discourse or sermon read or pronounced to an audience.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness.
scriptures: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
corruption_summary: A Carolingian counsellor who told kings they were under the law of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What is honourable in Smaragdus is the conviction, common to the best Carolingian writers, that rulers are servants of God and answerable to His law: “the throne is established by righteousness” (Pro 16:12). What must be named is the monastic frame around it, in which the higher Christian life is the cloistered one and the ordinary calling is the lower.

On the procession of the Spirit he stood with the Western church, and the text it rests on is Christ's own promise of the Comforter “whom I will send unto you from the Father” (John 15:26). The principle to recover is the one his King's Way assumes: that Scripture governs the magistrate, and that a king who will not read the law of God will not long keep it.
roots_summary: Hebrew melek (H4428), king; torah (H8451), law; Greek ekporeuomai (G1607), to proceed.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call, read aloud; Deuteronomy 17:19.
Greek ekporeuomai (G1607) — to go forth, proceed; John 15:26.
usage: “he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19) — the king under the book.
“Be wise now therefore, O ye kings” (Psa 2:10) — the mirror for princes in one line.
“the throne is established by righteousness” (Pro 16:12) — the foundation of rule.

pos: n. (Leporius, a monk of Gaul in the 420s, corrected by Augustine, author of the Libellus emendationis)
etymology: Latin Leporius, from lepus, a hare, or lepos, charm.
biblical_def: Leporius was a monk and presbyter in southern Gaul who, some years before Nestorius, taught a Christology that divided the Saviour. Unwilling to say that God was born of Mary or that God suffered, he spoke of a man joined to God, so that the Son of God and the son of Mary were two who acted together rather than one Person in two natures. He was also charged with Pelagian confidence in human ability. Censured by Proculus of Marseilles and other Gallic bishops, he went to Africa, where Augustine and Aurelius of Carthage reasoned with him, and he was persuaded. His Libellus emendationis, the little book of correction, is a public retraction: he confessed that the Word Himself was made flesh, that the one Christ is God and man, and that he had erred. When Nestorius taught the same error, John Cassian appealed to Leporius' retraction as the West's answer already given. The text he came to confess is John 1:14: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The grace he received is in Pro 28:13: “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines retraction as the recalling of what has been said, and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.
webster_full: RETRAC'TION, n. The act of withdrawing something advanced, or changing something done; recantation.
HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
INCARNA'TION, n. The act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man; as the incarnation of the Son of God.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: A divided Christ before Nestorius — and a model retraction after it.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Leporius' first teaching as the error the church would condemn at Ephesus in 431: a Christ in whom the Son of God and the son of Mary are two subjects. It survives in every account that will speak of Jesus as a man in whom God was present, or as the best of men indwelt by the divine, but not as God the Son made man. Paul confessed the mystery without division: “God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16).

The second lesson is the rarer. Leporius was restored because brethren did what Gal 6:1 commands, “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” (Gal 6:1), and because he did what men of learning seldom do, and recanted in writing. A retraction is not a humiliation to be avoided but a confession to be honoured.
roots_summary: Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; skenoo (G4637), to tabernacle; katartizo (G2675), to restore.
roots_lines: Greek skenoo (G4637) — to dwell as in a tent; John 1:14.
usage: “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14) — one Person, not two joined.
“great is the mystery of godliness” (1Ti 3:16) — confessed, not explained away.
“whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13) — the grace of a retraction.

pos: n. (Lupus, bishop of Troyes c. 427–c. 478, companion of Germanus of Auxerre on the mission against Pelagianism in Britain in 429)
etymology: Latin lupus, a wolf; Troyes, from the Gallic tribe of the Tricasses.
biblical_def: Lupus left a monastic life at Lerins to become bishop of Troyes about 427 and held the see for some fifty years. In 429 a synod of Gallic bishops, answering an appeal from the British churches, sent him with Germanus of Auxerre to Britain, where the teaching of Pelagius had taken root. According to Constantius of Lyon's life of Germanus, the two bishops met the Pelagian party in a public assembly, preached in churches and in the open fields, and so answered their opponents from Scripture that the crowd could scarcely be restrained from violence against the heretics. Lupus is also remembered from the year 451, when Attila's Huns swept through Gaul. He went out to meet the king, and Troyes was spared, though Attila carried the bishop with him as a hostage as far as the Rhine before releasing him. Lupus was brother-in-law to Hilary of Arles and was honoured by Sidonius Apollinaris as the father of the Gallic bishops. The doctrine he carried to Britain is Paul's: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Pelagianism as the doctrines of Pelagius, who denied original sin and the necessity of grace.
webster_full: PELA'GIAN, n. A follower of Pelagius, a monk of the fourth century, who denied original sin, and asserted the doctrine of free will and the merit of good works.
HOS'TAGE, n. A person delivered to an enemy or hostile power, as a pledge to secure the performance of the conditions of a treaty.
MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent, usually the being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers, for transacting business.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
John 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: A Gallic bishop sent to Britain to contend for grace against Pelagius.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The mission of 429 is a reminder that Pelagianism is not a theory but a pastoral disaster, and that churches have always needed men sent to answer it in public. Jude's charge is the commission Lupus carried: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3).

The honest caveat is that the Gallic church which sent Lupus was itself soon divided over grace, and Lerins, his old monastery, became a centre of the semi-Pelagian reaction against Augustine. The principle to recover is that grace must be confessed whole. A sinner is “justified freely by his grace” (Rom 3:24), and a mission that defends grace against Pelagius but softens it for the monk at home has fought half the battle.
roots_lines: Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; Romans 3:24.
usage: “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — the doctrine taken to Britain.
“Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom 3:24) — the answer to Pelagius.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jude 1:3) — the commission of 429.

pos: n. (Maurice, Roman emperor at Constantinople 582–602, to whom Gregory the Great protested the title of universal bishop)
biblical_def: Maurice was a Cappadocian general who became emperor in 582 and governed the eastern empire for twenty years through war with Persia and the Avars. He enters church history through the letters of Gregory the Great. When John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, used the title ecumenical patriarch in the acts of a synod, Gregory wrote to Maurice in 595 protesting that no bishop may call himself universal, and that whoever claims to be universal priest is in his pride the forerunner of Antichrist. Gregory also protested Maurice's law forbidding soldiers and officials to enter monasteries. In 602 the army rose under the centurion Phocas; Maurice fled, was taken, and was made to watch his five sons executed before he was beheaded himself. Gregory then wrote Phocas a letter of fulsome welcome, and in 607 Phocas granted Boniface III the very title Gregory had condemned. The episode is the papacy's own testimony against its later claims. Christ's rule for His ministers is Mat 20:26: “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an emperor as the sovereign of an empire, and a patriarch in the church as a dignitary superior to an archbishop.
webster_full: EM'PEROR, n. The sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; a title of dignity superior to that of king.
PA'TRIARCH, n. In the Christian church, a dignitary superior to the order of archbishops.
UNIVERS'AL, a. All; extending to or comprehending the whole number, quantity or space.
scriptures: But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
corruption_summary: The emperor whose reign produced a pope's own condemnation of the universal bishop.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the title of universal bishop as corruption on the testimony of a bishop of Rome. Gregory's letters to Maurice argued from the Gospel that no minister of Christ may claim lordship over the whole church, because Christ forbade His disciples the honours of the Gentile kings: “he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Luk 22:26). Roman apologists who explain that Gregory objected only to Constantinople's use of the title must explain why a title that marked the forerunner of Antichrist in 595 became the prerogative of Peter's chair in 607.

Maurice himself is a reminder that the magistrate is “the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) and is to be honoured, but not courted. Gregory's flattery of Phocas, a usurper with the blood of six men on his hands, shows how quickly the church that will not bow to the emperor in doctrine bows to him in politics. Christ's word stands over both: “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
usage: “let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26) — greatness in Christ's kingdom.
“he beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4) — the emperor's office.
“all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8) — no universal bishop.
